about: Chapter 13, Animal Jumps: 69 patterns, four for each of the 15 skills (1 and 2 marks), three 3-mark and three 5-mark long answers in steps (#208), and three 4-mark case studies, drawn from the chapter's 500 questions. All DRAFT until Ashalatha approves them.

patterns.text: A multiplier box changes {a} into {a * m}. What number does it multiply by?
patterns.hint: Which number times {a} makes {a * m}?
patterns.explanation: {a} × {m} = {a * m}, so the box multiplies by {m}.
patterns.misconception: Reverses factor and multiple language or assumes every smaller number is a factor.
patterns.notes: Inputs and multipliers 2 to 12 (different).

patterns.text: A multiplier box multiplies every input by {m}. Its output is {a * m}. What was the input?
patterns.hint: Undo the box: divide the output by {m}.
patterns.explanation: {a * m} ÷ {m} = {a}, because {m} × {a} = {a * m}.
patterns.misconception: Reverses factor and multiple language or assumes every smaller number is a factor.
patterns.notes: Multipliers 3 to 12, inputs 6 to 25.

patterns.text: Which number is a multiple of {r.n}?

wrong.mistake: picks a factor of {r.n} instead of a multiple
picks a number next to a multiple
picks a number that {r.n} does not divide exactly

patterns.hint: A multiple of {r.n} is {r.n} times a whole number.
patterns.explanation: {r.c} = {r.n} × {r.c // r.n}, so {r.c} is a multiple of {r.n}.
patterns.misconception: Reverses factor and multiple language or assumes every smaller number is a factor.
patterns.notes: Numbers 3 to 12 with a factor between 1 and the number, so 3, 5, 7 and 11 are not used; the multiple is 3 to 9 times it.

patterns.text: A multiplier box multiplies by {m}. Its output is {a * m}. What was the input? Show in your working how you checked your answer.
patterns.hint: Divide to undo the box, then multiply to check.
patterns.misconception: Reverses factor and multiple language or assumes every smaller number is a factor.
patterns.notes: Multipliers 4 to 12, inputs 11 to 30.

patterns.text: {r * c} chairs are set out in {r} equal rows. How many chairs are in each row?
patterns.hint: The rows and the chairs in a row are a factor pair of {r * c}.
patterns.explanation: {r} × {c} = {r * c}, so each row has {c} chairs.
patterns.misconception: Counts only one orientation or treats addends as factors.
patterns.notes: 2 to 9 rows of 3 to 12 (different).

picks a number without checking it against the statement

patterns.hint: Find a number the statement is about, for which it is false.
patterns.explanation: {r.why}, so the statement is false.
patterns.misconception: Accepts a pattern from one example as always true without checking a counterexample.
patterns.notes: Three claims: all factors of an even number are even; every multiple of an odd number is odd; every number divisible by 5 is divisible by 10. Wrong options share the parity of the right one, so odd/even gives nothing away.

wrong.mistake: adds the cycle lengths
finds the greatest common factor instead
subtracts or multiplies without checking

patterns.hint: The day must be a multiple of both {r.a} and {r.b}.
patterns.explanation: The next joint day is the first common multiple of {r.a} and {r.b}, which is {lcm(r.a, r.b)}.

patterns.notes: As S14-P1.

patterns.text: A bird feeder is filled every {r.a} days and cleaned every {r.b} days. Both are done today, day 0. On how many days from day 1 to day {r.N} are both done? Show in your working which days they are.

steps.text: Both are done every {r.l} days (the first common multiple of {r.a} and {r.b}).
Lists the days {r.l}, {2 * r.l} … up to {r.N}: {r.k} days.

patterns.hint: Find how often both happen together, then count up to day {r.N}.
patterns.explanation: Both are done every {r.l} days; up to day {r.N} that is {r.N} ÷ {r.l} → {r.k} days.
patterns.misconception: Adds the cycle lengths or counts the starting day as the first completed cycle.
patterns.notes: As S14-P1, days 60 to 120.

patterns.text: A jumper starts at 0 and makes equal jumps, each bigger than 1. How many different jump sizes land exactly on {r.t} without ever landing on {r.x}? A single jump straight onto {r.t} counts too.
patterns.hint: The jump size must be a factor of {r.t} that is not a factor of {r.x}.
patterns.explanation: Factors of {r.t} above 1 that do not divide {r.x}: {r.ok}. That is {r.k}.
patterns.misconception: Checks only the destination and forgets intermediate landing positions or forbidden targets.
patterns.notes: Targets 18 to 96 with at least four factors above 1; the number to avoid is below the target and rules out at least one but not all but one.

patterns.text: A jumper starts at 0 and must land exactly on {r.t} without ever landing on {r.x}. All its jumps are the same size, and bigger than 1. What is the smallest jump size it can use?
patterns.hint: Try the factors of {r.t} from the smallest. Skip any that divides {r.x}.
patterns.explanation: Jump sizes that work: {r.ok}. The smallest is {r.m}.
patterns.misconception: Checks only the destination and forgets intermediate landing positions or forbidden targets.

patterns.text: A jumper starts at 0 and makes equal jumps. It must land exactly on {r.t} but never on {r.x}. Which jump size works?

parts.text: (a) On which day do they next swim together?
parts.explanation: The first common multiple of {r.a} and {r.b} is {r.l}: day {r.l}.
parts.hint: Day 0 does not count: start counting from day 1.

parts.text: (b) On how many days from day 1 to day {r.N} do they swim together?
parts.explanation: The joint days are the multiples of {r.l}: {r.N} ÷ {r.l} → {r.j} days.
parts.hint: Day 0 does not count: start counting from day 1.

parts.text: (c) How many times does {who.name} swim from day 1 to day {r.N}?
parts.explanation: {r.N} ÷ {r.a} → {r.na} times.

parts.text: (d) How many times does the friend swim from day 1 to day {r.N}?
parts.explanation: {r.N} ÷ {r.b} → {r.nb} times.

parts.text: (e) Which numbers are the days when they swim together?

adds the two cycles
uses only one swimmer's days

parts.explanation: Swimming days are multiples of {r.a} and of {r.b}; days together are the common multiples, the multiples of {r.l}.

parts.text: (a) How many jump sizes land exactly on {r.t}?
parts.explanation: The jump sizes are the factors of {r.t} above 1: {r.nr} of them.
parts.hint: A jump size reaches {r.t} only if it divides {r.t}.

parts.text: (b) How many of those sizes never land on {r.x}?
parts.explanation: Sizes that divide {r.x} land on it ({r.bad}); the rest are {r.ok}: {r.nok} of them.

parts.text: (c) What is the smallest jump size that reaches {r.t} without landing on {r.x}?
parts.explanation: The sizes left are {r.ok}; the smallest is {r.m}.

parts.text: (d) How many jumps does that smallest size take to reach {r.t}?
parts.explanation: {r.t} ÷ {r.m} = {r.jm} jumps.

thinks small jumps cannot reach far
counts the jumps instead of checking where they land

patterns.stimulus: Case study: In a jumping game, a frog jumps {r.a} at a time and a rabbit jumps {r.b} at a time. Both start at 0 and the finish line is at {r.t}.

parts.text: (a) How many jumps does the frog make to reach the finish line?
(b) How many jumps does the rabbit make to reach the finish line?
(c) What is the first place after 0 where both land?
parts.explanation: The first common multiple of {r.a} and {r.b} is {r.l}.

parts.text: (d) Does the rabbit land on {r.x}?

wrong.mistake: gets the division wrong
thinks every place before the finish line is landed on
checks the frog's jump instead of the rabbit's

parts.explanation: {r.x} ÷ {r.b} = {r.x // r.b} remainder {r.x % r.b}, so {r.yn}.

patterns.misconception: Rounds the quotient and claims a target is reachable despite a remainder.
patterns.notes: Frog 2 to 7, rabbit 3 to 10 (neither divides the other); the finish is the second or third common multiple; part (d) is about a number the frog does not land on; half the answers are Yes.

parts.text: (a) How many children are in each team?
parts.explanation: The greatest common factor of {r.a} and {r.b} is {r.g}.

parts.text: (b) How many girls' teams are there?
(c) How many boys' teams are there?
(d) If the teams did not have to be as big as possible, which other team size would also leave nobody out?

picks a size that fits the boys only

patterns.notes: 24 to 72 children of each, the greatest common factor having another factor above 1 for part (d).

parts.text: (a) On which day are both held together next?
parts.explanation: The first common multiple of {r.a} and {r.b} is {r.l}.

parts.text: (b) On how many days from day 1 to day {r.N} are both held?
parts.explanation: Every {r.l} days: {r.N} ÷ {r.l} → {r.N // r.l}.

picks a fair day only
